hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? on your happiest days, does someone you miss ever come to mind?
options: then this custom was made for you. listen.
then you know the feeling this story keeps. listen.
good. keep this one for the day it happens.

steps.line: The Talmud tells of a rabbi named Mar, son of Ravina, who made a wedding feast for his son, long ago in Babylon.
The guests were great rabbis. And as the night went on, the celebrating got louder, and wilder.

steps.q: Mar sees the party getting out of hand, and reaches for something to break. What do you guess it is?
o: A jar of the feast’s wine
steps.why: A cup worth four hundred zuz, the Talmud says: a small fortune. A cheap jug wouldn’t have stopped anyone.

steps.line: So Mar brought out a precious cup, worth a fortune, and held it up for everyone to see.
And in front of all his guests, he broke it.
The room went still. The guests grew serious. The joy was still there, but now it remembered.

steps.q: Same page of the Talmud: at another wedding, the rabbis asked a sage to sing. What did he sing?
o: “Woe to us, for we will die”
A song about the bride’s beauty
A psalm of thanks for the harvest
steps.why: Rav Hamnuna Zuti sang “woe to us, for we will die” at a wedding. Same idea, sharper: one serious note inside the happiest night.

steps.line: Later teachers tied the custom to Jerusalem and its Temple, destroyed long ago. An old psalm says: keep Jerusalem above your highest joy.
Today, at the end of many Jewish weddings, under the wedding canopy, a glass wrapped in cloth is broken underfoot. Then everyone shouts, “Mazel tov!”
steps.label: today

steps.q: Many grooms say a verse just before the glass breaks. Which one?
steps.why: The same Psalm 137: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill.” “Next year in Jerusalem” ends the Passover meal; “pray for the peace of Jerusalem” is Psalm 122.

steps.q: Families tell it different ways. Match each reading.
pairs: something in the world is still broken
a glass that can’t be unbroken
an old way to scare off bad luck
steps.why: A Jewish wedding is happy to hold more than one meaning at once.

say: here’s what i love. nobody cancels the party. the cheering comes right after the crunch.
in jewish tradition, even the happiest day keeps a little room for what’s missing. traditionally the groom breaks the glass; at many weddings today either partner does, or both together.

steps.q: Mar’s cup was worth a fortune. Most weddings today use a simple glass. From the story, does that change the point?
o: Yes, it only works if it hurts to lose
No, the point is the pause, not the price
Yes, today it’s only for good luck
steps.why: Mar wanted a moment of seriousness in the middle of the joy. Any glass can give you that.

today.say: next time you celebrate something, even something small, take one quiet second for what’s still broken in the world, or for someone who isn’t there. then cheer.
options: even in joy, remember. then mazel tov.
then they’re part of today too. hold them gently.
